title: WHOM SHALL I SEND?
paragraphs:
WHOM SHALL I SEND?
A Question That Changes Destinies
There are moments when heaven asks a question that echoes louder than every voice on earth.
Not a question about status, influence, credentials, popularity, wealth, or human qualifications.
A question that has altered the course of nations, redirected generations, transformed ordinary people into history-makers, and turned scandals into testimonies.
A question that still echoes through eternity.
"Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" (Isaiah 6:8)
Most people read that verse as a beautiful line from Scripture.
Few realize it is one of the most dangerous questions God can ever ask a human being.
Because once you truly hear it, your life can never remain the same.
The prophet Isaiah was not attending a conference.
He was not sitting comfortably in a synagogue.
He was not listening to a sermon.
He was standing before the terrifying holiness of God.
"וָאֶשְׁמַע אֶת־קוֹל אֲדֹנָי אֹמֵר אֶת־מִי אֶשְׁלַח וּמִי יֵלֶךְ־לָנוּ"

Va'eshma et qol Adonai omer:
"Et-mi eshlach umi yelekh lanu?"
"And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?'"
The word "אֶשְׁלַח" (eshlach) comes from the Hebrew root שָׁלַח (shalach), meaning to send forth with purpose, commission, and authority.
God was not asking for a volunteer.
He was looking for a vessel.
Someone willing to carry heaven's burden into a broken world.
But before Isaiah could answer the question, something happened that many modern believers overlook.
"Woe is me! For I am ruined." (Isaiah 6:5)
In the presence of perfect holiness, Isaiah suddenly saw himself clearly.
The closer people come to God, the less impressive they become in their own eyes.
That is why genuine encounters with Christ produce humility rather than self-exaltation.
The things no one else could see.
And that is where many destinies stall.
But they do not want the cleansing.
Yet heaven's order has never changed.
Isaiah's lips were touched by a burning coal from God's altar.
"Your guilt is taken away and your sin atoned for."
Only after grace came the question.
This is one of the most beautiful patterns in all of Scripture.
God did not ask Isaiah to earn forgiveness.
God did not send Isaiah because he was perfect.
God sent Isaiah because he had been transformed.
That pattern reaches its fullest expression in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not the story of qualified people earning God's approval.
It is the story of disqualified people receiving God's mercy.
The Apostle Paul understood this better than most.
Before becoming Christianity's greatest missionary, he was hunting Christians.
Before writing Scripture, he was persecuting those who followed Jesus.
Before planting churches, he was destroying them.
His story should have ended in disgrace.
The Greek text of 1 Timothy 1:15 records:

Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς ἦλθεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον
ἁμαρτωλοὺς σῶσαι
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners."
Even after becoming an apostle, Paul never forgot what grace rescued him from.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
The greatest missionaries were often former rebels.
The most powerful testimonies frequently emerge from the deepest failures.
The strongest witnesses are often people who know exactly how much they have been forgiven.
This is why our theme remains timeless:
The Bible is filled with people who answered heaven's question.
Mary Magdalene carried a painful past.
Not because of what they had been.
Because of what His grace could make them become.
The Greek word translated "new" in Revelation 21:5 is:
It means renewed in quality, transformed, made different from what it once was.
That is exactly what Christ does with surrendered lives.
Perhaps that is why the question of Isaiah still pierces hearts today.
Because deep inside, most people know God is calling them toward something greater than comfort.
The question is not whether God is still calling.
The question is whether we are still listening.
Some are being called to share the Gospel.
Some are being called to forgive.
Some are being called to repent.
Some are being called to serve.
Some are being called to return after years of wandering.
Some are being called to surrender the very thing they have refused to place on the altar.
And somewhere in the quiet places of the soul, the question remains:
Availability has always been more valuable to God than self-confidence.
The Kingdom has never advanced primarily through the gifted.
Long after earthly applause fades, eternity remembers those who answered God's call.
And perhaps that is why this ancient question still changes destinies.
Because every human life eventually arrives at a crossroads.
One path ends in temporary comfort.
The other ends in eternal significance.
The other gives it away for the glory of God.
The One who deserved heaven's throne entered humanity's suffering.
The One without sin carried our sin.
The One who deserved worship embraced a cross.
The One rejected by men became the Savior of the world.
The cross is God's eternal declaration that no past is beyond redemption.
That truth is still transforming lives today.
Maybe you have spent years believing your mistakes define you.
Maybe you think heaven would never use someone like you.
Because the Gospel has always been God's story of taking broken people and making them beautiful through grace.
And perhaps today, the question is not merely for Isaiah.
The answer that changes destinies is still the same.
If this message stirred something deep inside your spirit, do not rush past it.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Supporting this ministry helps expand the reach of biblical content, discipleship resources, and faith-building materials for people around the world who desperately need the hope of Jesus Christ.
Because one surrendered "yes" can echo through generations you may never meet.
